proposition.text: Under the law as it stood prior to the enactment of s. 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act, by Act XX of 1929, the question whether the mortgagor in possession had power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent of the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. It has to be determined general principles and not the distinction between an English mortgage and a simple mortgage or the considerations germane to s.66 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the true position is that the mortgagor in possession may make a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of management; for instance, he may create a tenancy from year to year in the case of agricultural lands or from month to month in the case of houses. But it is not competent to him to grant a lease unusual terms or to alter the character of the land or to authorise its use in a manner, or for a purpose, different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. And it is for the lessee, if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee, to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management.

content.value: The mortgagor may make a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of management (e.g., tenancy from year to year for agricultural lands or month to month for houses).

The mortgagor is not competent to grant a lease unusual terms, alter the character of the land, or authorise its use in a manner or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage.
It is for the lessee to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee.

content.value: Section 66 is a statutory enactment of the powers of the mortgagor in possession in regard to waste of mortgaged property.
The mortgagor in possession is not liable for permissive waste (omission to repair or prevent natural deterioration).

The mortgagor is liable for destructive waste (acts which are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged property if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts).

proposition.text: A mortgagor in possession is liable for destructive waste, which consists of acts that are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged property if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts.

content.value: The liability applies if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by the acts.
The liability does not extend to permissive waste (omission to repair or prevent natural deterioration).

issues.explanation: The proposition text 'The mortgagee is not normally bound...' is a direct quote from L155, but the assertion_type 'OBLIGATION' is incorrect for a general rule of law stating what is 'not normally' the case. It should be 'LEGAL_PROPOSITION' or 'FACT' regarding the general rule. Furthermore, the source L155 is the primary source for this text, but the attribution includes L37 and L39 which are metadata. The core assertion is a legal principle, not an obligation imposed on a specific party in this context.
The record lacks the crucial qualification found in L155 ('But if a mortgagee takes his security with knowledge... he will be bound'). Without this exception, the proposition is incomplete.

events.source_basis: L155 contains the full text: 'The mortgagee is not normally bound by the acts of the mortgagor... But if a mortgagee takes his security with knowledge... he will be bound...'

L156 explicitly states the condition and the result: 'But if a mortgagee takes his security with knowledge of the purposes to which the land is applied and allows the mortgagor to remain in possession he will be bound by the acts done by the mortgagor in accordance with the usual course.'

L157 states: 'Consequently, if the mortgagor, after he has granted the mortgage, deals with the property in the usual course of management, the interest created by him may be rightly deemed operative against the mortgagee.'

L158 provides the examples: 'An illustration of this view is found in the ease of Moreland v. Richardson... The mortgagor could thus in the usual course of management create a ten- ancy from year to year in the case of agricultural land or from month to month in the case of property consisting of houses...'

L160 states: 'The mortgagor could thus in the usual course of management create a ten- ancy from year to year in the case of agricultural land or from month to month in the case of property consisting of houses and his dealings with the mortgaged property in the usual course of management would be operative against the mortgagee.'
L162 states: 'Whether the mortgagor possesses any larger powers of leasing is however very questionable.'

L163 states: 'It is only said that a mortgagor is not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing takes place to impair the value of the mortgagee's security the mortgagor does not exceed his powers in making a lease for a term.'

L164 states: 'It is only said that a mortgagor is not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing takes place to impair the value of the mortgagee's security the mortgagor does not exceed his powers in making a lease for a term.'

L173 states: 'The true position thus is that the mortgagor in possession may make a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of management... But it is not competent to the mortgagor to grant a lease unusual terms... And it is for the lessee... to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms...'

L175 states: 'The Court was really guided by the consideration that the mortgagor dealt with the property in the usual course of management and the interest which was thus created by the mortgagor in the usual course must rightly be deemed operative against the mortgagee.'
L177 states: 'The case of Banee Pershxd v. Beet Bhunjan Singh(1) therefore is really no authority for the wide proposition that a mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property...'
L179 states: 'The Court was really guided by the consideration that the mortgagor dealt with the property in the usual course of management...'
L180 states: 'The case of Banee Pershad v. Beet Bhunjan Singh(1) therefore is really no authority for the wide proposition...'

L181 states: 'In our opinion cite14†section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act has nothing to do with the mortgagor's power to lease the mortgaged property. cite14†Section 66 is a statutory, enactment of the powers of the mortgagor in.possession in regard to waste of mortgaged property.'
